subsubtopic: LAUNCHING OF LITHOPROBE PROJECT TO STUDY EARTH'S CRUST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) and the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines (Mr. Merrithew) together with NSERC have announced a five-year $25 million research project to investigate, using the latest in high technology equipment, the earth's upper crust. This project, known as Lithoprobe, was five years in the planning and will require extensive field experiments in four regions of the country. Some of Canada's best young scientists in our universities, government, and industry will be involved in one of the largest such projects ever undertaken in Canada. The four regions of experiment are the southern Cordillera in B.C., the Abitibi-Grenville greenstone belt in Quebec and Ontario, the Kapuskasing region in Ontario, and Newfoundland.
The project will concentrate on structural and earth forming processes, but the findings will be of long-term value in leading the way to hidden mineral and oil deposits in Canada, thus ensuring our economic future.

subsubtopic: NON-PAYMENT OF TAXES BY HIGH INCOME EARNERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, every day hundreds of thousands of Canadians buy lottery tickets with the hope of hitting a tax-free jackpot.
Yesterday Revenue Canada released a report which shows that you do not have to win a lottery to beat the tax man, all you have to do is be rich enough to afford a good tax lawyer or tax accountant. The recent report cites figures that show that in the latest taxation year for which figures are available there were 1,830 Canadians who earned over $100,000 per year and who paid not one cent in income tax. In other words, they hit the jackpot. This Government allowed them to make the windfall because it is not interested in closing loopholes like

subsubtopic: INCORRECT REPORT ON CRIMINAL CODE PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am concerned about a recent news item which distorted the facts concerning Canada's abortion law. In reporting the case of an Alberta teenager seeking an abortion over her parents' objections, the national media stated erroneously or otherwise that Canadian law allows abortion only up to 20 weeks of gestation. This was reported on CBC radio, and in local and national publications.
As all Members of the House know, Section 251 of the Criminal Code, our unfortunate abortion law, makes no reference to any legal time limit on so-called therapeutic abortions. What individual hospitals may choose to prohibit is separate from what the law allows. If a doctor can be found who is willing to perform the procedure, an abortion could be performed at nine months.
I call upon the national media to correct this appalling fact, and to stop spreading misinformation aimed at making the killing of unborn children more socially acceptable.

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
PRESENTATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour of tabling, in both official languages, the Second Report of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture. The report is entitled: Taxation of artists and the arts. The Committee asks the Government to table a response to its report, pursuant to Standing Order 99(2). The Committee has started to examine a number of important issues relating to Canada's cultural policy, and one of its priorities is to make the position of artists and the arts a more equitable one.

The key recommendation of the report is to incorporate a definition of professional artist and artistic activity in the Income Tax Act, a measure which would give juridical status to artists and their work. This measure would give the current administrative practice followed by Revenue Canada the force of law.
Other recommendations deal with the highly distinctive economic circumstances of artists. One of these, if adopted, would extend to professional artists the right to use block averaging and the modified accruals basis of accounting in the same way as do farmers and fishermen.
The needs of organizations established to promote the arts and the welfare of artists are also the subject of our recommendations, as is the larger issue of deductibility of charitable donations.
[ Translation]
The changes the committee is recommending have been considered at length and have received the unanimous approval of members of the arts world and of committee members representing the three federal political parties. Artists are hoping that changes in the legislation will be announced shortly. I would like to take this opportunity to thank Members from all three parties for their sustained effort in preparing this unanimous report for submission to the House.

subtopic: SOFTWOOD LUMBER PRODUCTS EXPORT CHARGE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to avail myself of this opportunity to speak for a few minutes on the export tax which is being imposed upon softwood lumber.
During an intervention yesterday by the Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Gormley), he suggested

January 21, 1987
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
that the woods industry in northern Saskatchewan was supportive of and happy with the imposition of the tax. The Hon. Member said that he had been in that area during the last few weeks. I suggest that he should return to northern Saskatchewan and ask mill operators and workers about the tax now that they have had a chance to look at it and its effects. In fact, the entire woods industry in northern Saskatchewan now recognizes the negative effect of the tax.
Of course the market has not settled down because of the change in tax. However, there is no doubt that the industry is already adjusting to its inability to fit into the market which will be developed by the imposition of the tax. Even now in places like Hudson Bay, Big River, and Meadow Lake-and two of these areas are in the Hon. Member's constituency- people recognize that they are unable to compete with the B.C. market for the areas that have traditionally been the direction in which their lumber has gone. In fact, a Hudson Bay plant which produces studs almost entirely and exports them to a great extent to the United States, particularly the Chicago market, is indicating that it laid off 30 employees because of the tax.
A study which was conducted in British Columbia suggested that the price of studs would be $120 per thousand, which is down about 25 per cent to 30 per cent from what it was before the tax was imposed. Also, the mill rate, or what the mill will get, is down from $153 per thousand to about $120 per thousand. Even with the transportation advantage in Saskatchewan of moving to the Prairies and possibly even to the Chicago market, no plant in Saskatchewan can match that rate. The lowest possible rate which can be matched in that province-and it would be very difficult to confirm it-is probably well above the $140 per thousand which B.C. companies suggest they can match anywhere in Saskatchewan.
Plants in Saskatchewan cannot possibly produce studs or lumber at that particular rate. Even the Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake should know that no plant in Saskatchewan has the ability to compete with the B.C. industry if it tries to sell into the Canadian market. A good portion of Saskatchewan production is sold domestically within Saskatchewan and within the Prairies. The rest of it is exported to the Chicago market or that particular part of the United States. Some of it is domestic production and goes to Ontario. However, no plant in Saskatchewan has the ability to compete with the B.C. industry. Therefore, the taxation imposed upon softwood lumber will directly and negatively affect the production of the mills in Saskatchewan. No doubt some of them will be able to adjust, but they will all feel the effects.
The reason Saskatchewan mills are unable to compete with the British Columbia industry has nothing to do with quality or even efficiency. We just do not have the scale of operations in Saskatchewan that there are in British Columbia. For instance, there is not one optimizer in any of the mills in Saskatchewan. The capital investment which would be necessary to put that kind of technology in place is so great
that no mill could afford it and stay operational. We do not have the world-class mills in Saskatchewan that are necessary to compete with British Columbia. We also have to take into consideration distance, the cost of wood and the transportation of wood to the mill. The cost of wood is so high to start with, having brought it out of the bush and to the mills, that the Saskatchewan mills already start with a disadvantage.
British Columbia mills have suggested that when they start selling into the new markets on the Prairies, in Ontario and in the United States, they will probably be forced to use the U.S. transportation system. If the Transportation Act, which is presently before this House, were to pass very suddenly- which we hope will not happen-it would allow Canadian companies to ship on U.S. transportation lines to U.S. markets. At present there is a requirement to cross the Canadian Prairies to reach the Ontario and U.S. markets.
In Saskatchewan, where we have a fairly large number of operations in places like Hudson's Bay, Big River, Meadow Lake and Prince Albert, this tax will affect us. Even where the market is domestic it will affect us. Other areas of Canada will be able to take over our market without too much difficulty. We will not be able to sell at the price which larger and more technically capable mills can from other provinces.
Management consultants studying the effect of this tax suggest that a large number of mills under the $153 a thousand or a little higher survived, but now they will be forced out of business. Jobs will be lost. We also know that with the little higher prices in the States, many mills will not be able to operate. With the added burden of the 15 per cent tax, many of those marginal mills in the U.S. will take over part of their own market. The total amount of lumber shipped to the United States will be considerably less than we expect it to be. Because lumber will be more expensive in the States this will translate into fewer U.S. housing starts. Not only will we have to pay 15 per cent more or take a 15 per cent drop in the price of lumber, because of the increased price in the United States we will not be selling the same amount of lumber as we have in the past.

subtopic: SOFTWOOD LUMBER PRODUCTS EXPORT CHARGE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to enter this debate today to point out some obvious problems with the export tax. The most crucial point of all is the very idea that the Parliament of Canada should be considering such action at all. We are not responding to any Canadian concern, we are merely responding to American pressure. We are considering a tax on the export of softwood lumber because the United States says we should. That more than anything else is clearly unacceptable to me, to my Party and, in a general sense, to the people of Canada.
This tax comes before us as a desperate, last-minute arrangement made by the Conservative Government. It shows. There are obvious inequities and oversights in this proposal, showing that it was rushed through without sufficient thought or planning.
For example, the original complaint from the American lumber industry was about low stumpage fees. This tax has nothing whatsoever to do with stumpage fees. Instead, this debate is about a tax on the export of softwood lumber products. It is not the right measure to address the American complaint. It takes a broad-brush approach and victimizes many innocent people.
The American countervailing duty was assessed on the first mill price. Although we argue that this countervailing action was unjust, at least it was aimed at what the Americans saw as being the problem. However, the Canadian export tax is not levied at the first mill. Fifteen per cent on the export price is charged as the softwood crosses the border. The proposal indicates that the free-on-board mill price paid or payable for the products includes all costs incurred to produce the products. That involves a lot more than just stumpage fees.
The Government's export tax assumes two things: that all softwood leaving the country is taxable and that it comes from the first mill. That may not be the case. Let me explain.
There is a lumber supplier in my constituency of Brant who imports American lumber, cuts and dresses it and sells it to construction companies in the northern United States. However, the regional director of tax interpretation in London, Ontario, has ruled that this supplier must pay 15 per cent of such a sale and he is right. I have searched in vain for some provision in this Bill that would exempt such a transaction. There is no such provision. This proposal simply indicates that softwood exported to the United States is taxable.
We are protecting Americans in respect to their own lumber. The measure does not address a complaint about Canadian stumpage fees. It just assures that re-manufacturing takes place on the American side of the border. Canadian suppliers to American markets will be forced to close or move their operations South. Canada will stop exporting softwood and start exporting jobs.
There are other inequities in this proposal as well. Some mills are exempt from the tax. This will force some mills out of business and give others a decided competitive advantage. This tax may not only lose Canadian jobs but may contribute to increased corporate concentration. In addition, Canadian suppliers buy from these exempt mills but if they turn around and sell the same lumber to the U.S. they have to pay the tax.
A supplier in my riding buys stock from Irving Lumber in New Brunswick. Irving Lumber is exempt from the tax. However, the Ontario supplier will be forced to pay the tax when he tries to move the lumber to market in the U.S. I understand some 120 companies in Canada have drawn these anomalies to the attention of the authorities.
I use the word "anomalies" because that is the word the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) used in response to my two questions in Question Period today on this very subject. She did not say I was wrong. She said these were anomalies which had crept in. That is another way of saying we goofed. We did not take the time to plan. We did not take the necessary degree of exactness in our negotiations to make certain these anomalies did not creep in.
There may be ways of addressing such inequities but the agreement prevents the Government from assisting the lumber industry. The Americans assert that the tax revenue cannot be used to benefit the lumber industry. They assert that stumpage fees were an unfair subsidy and were able to get the Canadian Government to accept that fact by bringing in this tax. How will Americans look on modernization grants or low-interest loans which Canada might offer its lumber industry? The Government has allowed the U.S. to stick its nose into our stumpage fees. Will regional development assistance be next?
There may be even wider consequences to this Government's caving in. This tax applies only to exports to the U.S. That is dangerous for two reasons. It is inconsistent with the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade because it applies only to the U.S. That opens the door for other countries to pursue the
January 21, 1987

same course of action. What is to prevent other producer countries from insisting that the tax apply to exports to their markets? After all, the Government has admitted our exports deserve to be taxed.
This tax invites more trouble and it will not come just from outside Canada. This tax is a recipe for federal, provincial and regional disputes. The export tax could be altered by a change in stumpage fees but stumpage fees are a provincial matter and the provinces have different levels of stumpage. Will all the provinces agree to raise their stumpage fees? Should stumpage fees be made uniform across the country? If only some provinces raise their stumpage fees will they not balk at paying the bill for lifting a federal tax? I do not envy the Prime Minister who has to negotiate such an agreement, whoever that person may be in a couple of years' time.
Finally, we should not kid ourselves that this tax is the end of the problem. I submit it is just the beginning. The Government has recognized that might makes right. The Americans have enormous economic power, therefore Canada has to jump when the Americans demand change, even if it infringes on our sovereignty and puts Canadians out of work. This is a very bad and dangerous precedent. There is no one in this House who can go home and face his or her constituents and tell them their jobs are safe. The Americans could suggest that any product exported from Canada will be next on the list. Canadians now know that the Government will not protect them from such an attack.
While this is an unfortunate cave-in, it may not be irreparable. If in a few years' time the next Government develops a degree of courage in facing up to the U.S., or any other country, it is possible that we may be able to bring in remedial legislation after the end of this Parliament. However, it is abundently clear to me that the present Government, in cosying up to the U.S. on a whole host of issues and disputes and problems, has weakened, not strengthened, our national identity, our Canadianess and our ability to cope with our problems. Witness the softwood lumber issue and our negotiations with a major power. No one ever said it was easy negotiating with the U.S. It never will be. However, if you negotiate from a position of weakness and on the premise that you have to give in at the outset of any negotiations, then God help us when it comes to other important issues in the future.

They are to open up the business relationship between Canada and the United States to give Canadian businesses wider access to the American markets.
We must keep in mind, however, that the reason we were in a countervail situation and had to negotiate the softwood lumber deal was because of the strong American dollar and the weaker Canadian dollar. The Canadian lumber producer did have a 38-cent advantage. In fact, because of the difference in the dollar, Canadian producers could charge the same price on the American market as it charged on the Canadian market and have a 35 per cent or 38 per cent advantage. That is what brought on the tension between the producers in the United States and those in Canada.
Due to this, there has been increased trade across the border, not only in lumber, but in all other industries which have been taking advantage of the market in the United States. Canadian industries have been able to strengthen their market positions in the United States because of the lower Canadian dollar. One plant in my constituency put on an extra
January 21, 1987

shift six or seven years ago when the dollar had dropped to about 80 cents. They believed that if the dollar stayed at that level or dropped further it would be profitable for them to run another shift and ship into the United States. They gambled that the Canadian dollar would remain weaker than its U.S. counterpart. They expanded their operation by employing another shift and have been doing very well. We are all happy for them.
1 believe that even Opposition Members would agree that, although there are a lot of down sides to having a weaker Canadian dollar, it is because of that lower dollar that our manufacturers have been able to compete better in the United States. The fact is that this profitability has allowed our plants to improve and modernize and, consequently, in many cases, to be able to compete more effectively in the U.S. market. That is the good side of it.
In addition, this deal allows producers to plan. It is a fact that there has been insecurity in the forest industry in Canada for the past three years because it did not know how the American industry would respond to Canadian success. What we needed was a firm deal with the United States. It may be that we all wish that would not have been necessary, but the fact is that it was necessary. The Canadian industry now has a package which provides it with a framework which it knows will be in place and which allows it to plan its business in such a way that it can predict and anticipate the future. The clearest example of that was given by the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) the other day.
In the last days of December the stock market showed stock prices of some of the manufacturers as being 28 per cent below what it was after the deal. That is, after the deal the stocks of the leading manufacturers and lumber in Canada rose dramatically because the investors knew exactly where they were at and they could plan. They moved from a period of insecurity to a period of security. The deal allows investors to respond in a systematic way to U.S. competition.
Third, it is a good deal because it allows for adjustments to correct anomalies. The Hon. Member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) pointed out that there are anomalies. All of us recognize that. There are members of the industry, particularly in the remanufacturing sector, who face anomalies and who will face a 15 per cent disadvantage in some of the product lines they manufacture. Members of the Opposition have failed to point out, however, is that that list was compiled in the last days of the negotiation by the legal council of the remanufacturers from a list supplied to them by the remanufacturers. Members will turn to Clause 8(d), they will see that the Canadian negotiators allowed for that kind of variable. Clause 8 (d) reads:

Members from British Columbia know that there is a lot to be done in British Columbia to bring the forest industry up to par so that we can continue to harvest that resource in the years ahead. An American countervail duty, the Canadian export tax or an increase in stumpage fees do not in any way, shape or form affect the selling price of a product. The selling price is set by the market based on a variety of factors, most particularly demand. When people are building homes they are buying two-by-fours. Mr. Speaker, I want to thank you for giving me the opportunity to take part in this most important debate on Bill C-37.

I feel compelled to express my views today on the current Bill relating to the 15 per cent export tax on softwood lumber exports to the United States.
As the Member for Timmins-Chapleau, representing a constituency of northern Ontario, I have a vested interest in ensuring the federal Government's endeavours in the softwood lumber issue are in the best interests of all Canadians, particularly those in northern Ontario.
At issue is a 15 per cent federal export tax imposed by the federal Government on all softwood lumber exported to the United States. Considering the following facts, the potential ramifications of the tax on northern Ontario are serious indeed.
Let us consider a brief profile of northern Ontario as it relates to the sawmill industry, 90 per cent of all wood cut in northern Ontario is softwood; 80 per cent of total softwood cut in Ontario is from the northern region of the province; 28 mills account for 85 per cent of the softwood lumber cut in Ontario;
6,000	people are directly employed in the sawmill industry with an annual payroll of $117 million.
In northern Ontario, we are painfully aware that northern Ontario's economy is largely resource based. There are communities that are totally reliant on softwood lumber. Therefore, as a Member of Parliament representing a constituency in northern Ontario, I am sensitive to the special needs and concerns of the residents of the region. The reality of the situation is that, if Canada had not pushed the U.S. into an agreement on softwood lumber, the Americans would have imposed their own countervailing duty. In fact, they had imposed a 15 per cent countervailing duty on Canadian softwood going into that country since October, 1986. The American countervailing duty, if implemented, would have been disastrous for Canada and northern Ontario.
If we had not pushed for an agreement, the United States could have imposed a higher countervailing duty, resulting in a loss of some $600 million. An American countervailing duty would deny all company exclusions. Under the countervailing duty process, the U.S. Commerce Department conducts annual reviews and can unilaterally determine the value of changes in provincial stumpage practices. The countervailing duty rate is established in these annual reviews and can be revised retroactively.
The actual level of the countervailing duty will vary with changes in the perceived subsidy level and would increase in a down market.
Under the negotiated agreement, the federal Government will return revenues to the provinces predicated on export performance. Under this plan, Ontario could conceivably earn from $35 million to $45 million based on export performance of the softwood producers. Eventually, replacement measures will be instituted by the provinces so that they can be responsible to collect the fees themselves.
From a northerner's perspective, I am pleased to hear that the Ontario Government plans to return its share of these funds collected by the federal Government to the northern region.

per cent export tax to retrain affected lumber workers. It may even set up a heritage fund for northern Ontario. I support these initiatives since the provincial Government appears to be in agreement with the federal Government's commitments to assisting northern Ontario.
I have many personal views of where these funds might be expended for the forestry sector in northern Ontario-first, on greater control of the spruce and jack pine budworms which have been devastating our forests for years; second, on a better and higher rate of reforestation; and, third, on the search for expanded international markets in Europe and the Pacific Rim in order that we are not totally reliant upon the United States markets.
I do not deny that a 15 per cent export tax on Canadian softwood will hurt softwood lumber producers in northern Ontario. The federal Government is concerned about potential ramifications to the industry. To this end, we have been in contact with the Canadian Forestry Service which is monitoring the activities of 28 sawmills across Ontario that account for 75 per cent of the softwood cut in Ontario. The survey will assist the federal Government in determining the impact of the 15 per cent export tax on the industry. We will be pleased to share the results of the survey and other information pertinent to the industry with the provincial Government of Ontario and with the industry.
In my riding of Timmins-Chapleau, I have communicated with all major softwood lumber producers in the region to discuss the 15 per cent export tax. The individuals involved in the industry are fiercely independent, hardworking people. They are sincerely devoted to free enterprise and are mature enough to understand the issue and draw their own reasonable conclusions. They are not ready to close down or lay off.
Some of them expressed concerns or reservations about the impact of the duty on the industry. However, all of them agree that it is better having the money remain in Canada as opposed to paying a duty to the United States. Now that the money will remain in Canada, it will be reinvested in our own country instead of providing the Americans with a financial windfall.
It is important to consider the nature of the softwood industry. It is a cyclical business, affected by many extenuating influences such as building starts and weather conditions. As a cyclical business it is prone to regular slow-downs and even shut-downs. During this period sawmill owners take advantage of the time to do other important related activities such as machinery maintenance, building maintenance, et cetera.
While I do not deny a tax increase is not altogether healthy for the softwood industry, or for any other industry for that matter, it is crucial to consider that the industry has periods when its productivity is reduced. This is a natural occurrence

I would like to discuss this Bill in terms of what it does to our relationship with the United States and to the sovereignty of Canada. Bill C-37 is entitled "an Act respecting the imposition of a charge on the export of certain softwood lumber products". My colleague, the Member for Humber- Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin), said that the Bill should be entitled "an Act respecting the imposition of the American administration's will on the weak and vacillating Tory administration in Canada".
Members on the Government side have said that Members of the Opposition do not like the Americans. That is not true at all. My father came to Canada at the age of nine years. He and my grandfather selected Canada as their home at that
time. My Dad passed away one year ago at the age of 94. He was a great Canadian.
I must say that most of my relatives are Americans. Actually about 75 per cent of my cousins live in the Massachusetts area. Therefore, I do not feel that I, or most members of the Opposition, have anything detrimental to say about the Americans. They have been good neighbours and good allies. Certainly Canada has done an awful lot during its history in conjunction with the United States. However, we all have good neighbours in our various localities. That does not mean we have to crawl into bed with them. We want our country to remain an independent sovereign nation.
1 look at this tax as an erosion of our sovereignty. There have been many indications of this erosion since this Government took power. There was the ice-breaker which moved through our northern waters without asking permission, not recognizing our sovereignty in the North. That was a very contentious issue. I know the Government did a lot of howling about it and I am sure the Canadian people in the last year or so, and as long as this Government is in power, will certainly take a tough stand when it comes to our sovereignty as it relates to the North and, certainly, as it relates to our country.
The softwood lumber export tax is a vitally important matter for many reasons. Of course, my colleagues have expounded upon those reasons at some length. I would like to expand on the subject with regard to the limits this sort of action puts upon Canada's ability to manage its own natural resources. Mr. Speaker, we find ourselves in debate today because the Canadian forest industry has been too successful in penetrating the United States market. The large disparity between the Canadian and the U.S. dollar, the efficiency of product and its quantity and quality, make the protectionist sentiment and action of the United States forest industry all but inevitable. Canadian forest companies have moved from 17 per cent to 33 per cent of the market.
The provinces should have adjusted their forest policies several years ago. They should have made adjustments regarding stumpage, annual allowable cut and intensive silviculture, recognizing the full implications of unneccessarily depleting a precious forest resource. They should have moved toward diversification, secondary manufacturing in the prime resource field. They should have had a stronger emphasis from industry and from provincial management many years ago. But again it is difficult to move from a status quo.
I suppose at this time it is time to compliment the unions because they in fact have seen this coming for several years and were among the first to call for changes in this direction. Back in 1983 the Minister of Transport was early to recognize protectionist forces in the United States and called for a comprehensive trade agreement. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), as soon as he took office, moved toward a comprehensive free trade with the United States because he recognized the tide of protectionism and immediately countered with his own free trade initiative. The provinces started talking but it was too little, too late. The first thing we knew another very serious, even deadly, countervailing duty was upon us. Through the mechanism of enhanced federal-provincial relationships, the provinces called upon the federal Government to help, and the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) came in and negotiated a better deal than even the money markets' managers could ever have contemplated. We are now implementing an interim measure export tax until our provinces can modernize and redesign their own forest policies. Until then, the federal Government will collect a tax for intensive silviculture and job retraining in the provinces.
Our Minister and her negotiators should be complimented and appreciated for their efforts with respect to the complicated agreement and negotiations which had to be completed on Canada's behalf. She has done a fine job for Canada, and Canadians are beginning to recognize this more and more each day.
There is a growing consensus among members of the industry, the unions, the financial community and British Columbians that the Government, facing a difficult situation to negotiate, has in fact done a good job in reaching a negotiated settlement. I get the feeling that the industry senses it can now live with the agreement. It now feels we should get on with settling the anomalies of the agreement as quickly as possible. That is really what this debate should be focused on and what subsequent committee meetings should be looking at in terms of giving priority to it.
During the parliamentary recess I was pleased to meet with many groups and representatives of the forest industry in British Columbia. Of particular importance were the meetings I held with the Independent Lumber Remanufacturers Association of British Columbia. The B.C. secondary softwood lumber industry is a sector of the forest industry which has grown in importance to the province in recent years. The industry has over 60 firms and employs close to 3,000 workers. In 1986, its sales volume was estimated to be in the range of $500 million Canadian.
The industry produces a wide range of value-added products from raw material purchased from primary lumber producers, both in British Columbia and the United States. The industry sells its products to both domestic and foreign markets. By far,

it is the most important market for many firms is the United States. This small but growing sector of the British Columbia lumber industry is of utmost importance to British Columbia and Canada because the remanufacture, secondary manufacture or value-added components of the forest industry are critical to the full use and management of Canadian forest resources.
The British Columbia economy is hurt by the buffeting of primary resource boom and bust cycles. It must be levelled out through a diversified secondary industry base, the most logical and natural part of which is the secondary manufacture of local primary resources.
Because of the importance of the remanufacturing sector, and because this sector finds anomalies in the agreement as it relates to them, I was pleased to welcome Mr. Shawn Sullivan of the Independent Lumber Remanufacturers Association and Mr. Charles Widman of the Coalition of British Columbia Secondary Softwood Lumber Manufacturers to meet with Ministers and members of the British Columbia caucus to discuss the anomalies of the agreement as it relates to their sectors. I am pleased to report that the delegations felt that they received a very good hearing from both the British Columbia caucus, the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines (Mr. Merrithew) and the officials in the Departments involved. Members of the delegations left with a slight glimmer of hope that, with minor adjustments, a resolution of their problems might be found in the interpretation and implementation of the agreement.
The application of the U.S. Coalition for Fair Lumber Imports was focused on a perceived competitive inequity caused by what it viewed as unfairly low stumpage rates paid by Canadian producers. Its complaints were not directed toward value-added activities through remanufacture. This position was clearly stated in its application and followed up in the agreement. Negotiators for the agreement wisely recognized that under the pressure of a tough deadline certain anomalies might arise in areas of the agreement. As a result Clause 4 b. was put into the agreement. It states in part:
The export charge however will not be imposed on the value added in manufacturing some softwood lumber products.
That is, of course, the key by which we will have to try to see if we can find space for some of the other products which were perhaps missed in the first place. The Independent Lumber Remanufacturers Association was pleased that the list of products it submitted appeared in the agreement, giving them protective exclusions. However, upon closer examination by all parties involved, it was recognized that a number of other products such as pallet cut stocks, bed frame components, firring strips, roof decking cedar boards and industrial clears and shop products of remanufactured, box shook, edge-glued panels, select fascia and other patterns, such as 134, 130, 116, 118, 137, 204 A&B, 206 and 141, under NLGA standard grading rules may have been inadvertently left off the list of exclusions.
Similarly, some companies which would have qualified under the corporate exclusion list had they applied were left off that particular list. Whether they did not know that they could apply, whether they knew and did not want to apply because of the risk involved or because of the paperwork effort, cost and exposure of their books, or whether they simply assumed that the matter would be settled before it affected them directly, there still exists an anomaly in the agreement. In the outcome some companies of equal standing have exclusions while others do not.
Undoubtedly, the negotiators of the United States are strong and competent. However, we must also assume that they are fair and want to correct any such anomalies that may have occurred under the pressure of time and a tight deadline. Certainly, when rough lumber that comes from the United States is sold to Canada and we treat it with wood preservatives and then send it back to the United States the Americans do not want to see us charging a duty on that since they surely must want us to continue to buy that raw lumber. Thus it will be in their best interests, as well as in ours, to have a look at some of these anomalies to see if we cannot find a satisfactory solution to them. I hope the Government will appeal to the sense of fair play well known to the United States ethic and in the interpretation and implementation of the agreement make adjustments to these anomalies in the positive spirit and intention of the agreement itself.
We must resolve this issue and move on quickly to a comprehensive free trade agreement with the United States.
